items.title: 333 Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH traffic and retrieve plaintext email
items.excerpt: Unknown hackers hijacked more than 300 Tor exit nodes and reconfigured them to favor unencrypted email traffic and redirect SSH connections through servers they controlled, a researcher reported Tuesday. The hijacking began in late August, when, according to Tor volunteers , the attacker used a valid password that had been reused to gain access to a Tor management server. The attacker then installed Ebury , a backdoor written for Linux that was discovered 12 years ago. Mysteries remain Then the attacker connected from the management server to a second Tor server, called Switzerland2, through SSH, using an RSA key that, for unknown reasons, investigators couldn’t find among Switzerland2’s authorized keys. With administrative control of Switzerland2, the attackers installed Ebury there as well. Finally, the attacker reconfigured settings on two exit nodes that Switzerland2 hosted. Read full article Comments

items.title: UN says we're going to blow past 1.5º warming, offers a "now what?" answer
items.excerpt: In 2015, all but two countries agreed to make an effort to keep global temperatures from reaching 1.5° C above pre-industrial readings. Since then, most of the world has largely treated what they signed on to as aspirational, and one of the largest emitters (the US) has alternately withdrawn and recommitted to the agreement. Meanwhile, the planet has responded as expected to steadily rising carbon emissions and appears to be practically at the 1.5° limit. On Wednesday, for the first time, the United Nations Environmental Programme (UNEP) acknowledged that reality , and conceded that the goal of keeping warming below 1.5° was no longer a viable one. Instead, its new goalposts focus on keeping both how long we exceed that limit and how much we exceed it by, at a minimum. Doing that will require both dramatic emissions cuts now and the removal of hundreds of gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere before the century is out. Bowing to the inevitable Depending on which baseline you use to establish pre-industrial temperatures, as well as which reconstruction of global temperatures you rely on, the world has either gotten very close to, or already exceeded the 1.5° milestone. The current El Niño event, which appears exceptionally strong, will almost certainly mean that we've gone over it no matter which records you choose. Read full article Comments

items.excerpt: Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr today warned broadcasters about airing "fake polls," amplifying one of the many complaints that President Trump has regularly made about the news media. Carr's post on X said, "Many journalists and broadcasters have been amplifying or airing these Polls without regard to basic journalistic ethics and without informing the public that those Polls lack a scientific, accurate, or even real basis... Broadcasters are advised to avoid engaging in News Distortions or running Broadcast Hoaxes by airing Polls that would violate their regulatory obligations." Carr urged broadcasters to "provide their viewers with additional context and information about Polls they have covered." In fact, one small polling outfit was exposed as a hoax this week, and a similar incident occurred in August. News outlets have reported on these hoaxes, providing the very "context" that Carr said is needed. Read full article Comments

items.title: Enterprises keep buying software upgrades that IT thinks will make things worse
items.excerpt: Enterprise-sized businesses spend, on average, 28 percent of their software budgets on unwanted upgrades, migrations, and licensing changes. Often, those firms' IT heads think those changes are detrimental. Those results are according to a survey of 2,018 chief information officers and senior IT decision-makers at companies with at least 10,000 employees that Origina commissioned for its report, “ The Software Tax .” About half of the respondents (1,011) are from the US, and the rest are from the United Kingdom. All respondents worked at companies with at least $1 billion in annual revenue. Keep in mind that Origina provides maintenance for various enterprise software. Its report points to independent software maintenance as a way for IT leaders to regain control over software budgets, illustrating its potential bias. A third-party research consultancy, Censuswide , conducted the survey. Read full article Comments

The code is a mess right now, but it'll get better I promise. You can also help with that. We didn't build this to make money. Just an excel sheet will do! But then the more we dug into it and tried different simulators, the more we realized that it's more complex than it looks. We even signed up to Pulley, Carta and others just to run simulations. But they're a bit confusing. TL;DR: Understanding modern startup funding and knowing how much dilution you'll face is hard. We built a tool that'll hopefully help with that. You can add Post-money Safes, priced rounds and issue options to employees, and you can see how that affects your ownership at every step. You can also simulate an Exit scenario and see how much money you'll be left with. --- Some examples of complex stuff: - There are many different types of safes. They all convert at the first priced round, but in different ways. items.title: Prompt Injection Is Just the Start of AI Agent Security (Here's What You Need)
items.excerpt: Learn more about agent security here: https://fandf.co/4i1Qs4u My second brain helps me run my entire business, and that means giving it access to a lot of my systems and data, so I check everything it pulls in and keep its access limited. That works for one agent. A company has agents running across cloud platforms and employee devices, and IT has to know which ones exist, who owns them, and what they can reach. Microsoft is expanding Project Perception, building on Agent 365, to secure AI agents at scale. It gives agents their own identity, scopes their access to the task, and contains them as risk changes, without taking away employees' approved access. Dynamic Permissions gives agents task-specific, time-bound access to supported resources, and separately, risk-based access controls evaluate supported agent actions using current risk and policy. Your team reviews and approves protections before they're enforced. Thanks to Microsoft for working with me on this!

items.title: 1,368 AI Failures and What They Teach About Evals — Vishal Srivastava & Tanmay Sah, New York Life
items.excerpt: Vishal Srivastava and Tanmay Sah studied 1,368 incidents from a public AI incident database to ask what real failures say about how AI systems should be tested. They sort failures across three areas (technical strength, deployment controls and business impact) and 13 sub-areas that cover about 98% of incidents. Weak deployment controls, such as human review and monitoring, are the most closely tied to harm. They show how to rank use cases by how much is at stake, why the evaluator itself needs checking, and a build-break-fix loop that tries to prove a system wrong instead of right, applied to a real airline chatbot that gave a customer the wrong refund policy. items.title: How to Test AI Agents When No Benchmark Exists — Nathanael Weill, Air Canada
items.excerpt: Nathanael Weill leads a team building AI agents at Air Canada, where tasks are so specific there's no public benchmark and domain experts have little time to grade results. His fix is to write the answer first: start from a known answer, generate the input from it, and check whether the agent finds its way back. He shows how that took a past RAG project from one expert-graded test a week to dozens of automated tests a day, then applies it to a supplier-contract review agent with five ways to build a test set: past decisions, planted rule violations, removed clauses, changes that shouldn't matter, and contract templates with filled-in blanks. He also explains why he avoids LLM judges whenever code can check the answer. items.title: Why AI Writing Still Reads Like Slop — Louis-François Bouchard, Towards AI
items.excerpt: Louis-François Bouchard of Towards AI breaks down what makes AI writing feel like slop: overused words, vague generalities, saying nothing, repetition, hallucination and a voice that sounds like everyone at once. He then shows how his team built a benchmark to measure whether a model can write a video script in his own voice: 10 scripts, 5 drafts per model, 4 LLM judges, nine scoring metrics and 1,000 human A/B checks. He shares what it cost, why judges favor their own model family, and practical tips for writing with AI: very long prompts full of examples, one review pass from a strong model, many cheap drafts merged together, and always a human edit. items.title: Does Code Quality Still Matter? It Depends on This — Max Kanat-Alexander, Capital One
items.excerpt: Every senior engineer's answer is "it depends." Max Kanat-Alexander says what it actually depends on. Code quality always existed for two things: understanding a system and safely changing it. AI is making a new kind of software common: disposable software, with low consequences, few dependents and near-zero cost to replace or maintain. For that software, quality doesn't matter. For durable software it matters more than ever. He also shows how to make systems more disposable and how to make rigor cheap through standards, in-workflow tooling, easy testing and maximum strictness. items.title: Alpenglow: Rebuilding Solana’s Consensus For Sub-Second Finality
items.excerpt: Alpenglow is live on Solana mainnet. Anza CEO Brennan Watt explains why the team started from ground zero to rebuild Solana's consensus, and what faster finality unlocks. "You can't iterate your way into a better consensus in a way that is safe and performant." – Brennan Watt Alpenglow replaces TowerBFT, the consensus protocol Solana has run since launch. Under TowerBFT, a block was final once a tower of votes stacked up over 32 slots, about 12.8 seconds. Alpenglow's new voting protocol, Votor, finalizes blocks in one or two rounds of voting and is built to bring finality down to ~150ms. For users, nothing changes: same apps, same wallets, same fees. They shouldn't have to notice Alpenglow. They'll just feel it. items.title: Exploring Unsupervised Methods for Recovering the Refusal Direction in LLMs
items.excerpt: Introduction This is the first part of what we plan to be a research exploration into the geometries of LLMs. We start with building off existing work by Arditi et al focused on the refusal direction in LLMs. Background We recommend reading the Arditi et al. Lesswrong post and paper for more details. They explore the idea of the behavior categorized as Refusal being mediated by a single direction. Refusal is basically when an LLM refuses to do something, so examples like "I cannot fulfill..." "I cannot complete..." etc. A direction is defined by a vector. Here, it means a vector in an LLM's activation space. An LLM's activation space is the space where an LLM's internal vectors live. Think of the intermediary vectors that are used in the calculation of the final next-token-prediction process. Mediated means that if this direction were to be removed, then the behavior categorized as Refusal would stop. Arditi et al. performs directional ablation as their method of removal. They identify the refusal direction using difference-in-means . Methodology We apply Principal Component Analysis and Isomap alongside diff-in-means to an experimental setup of refusal. We test the Llama 8b 3.1 Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct models. items.title: What's in CODI's latent recurrent thoughts?
items.excerpt: What's in CODI's latent recurrent thoughts? TL;DR CODI is a model using latent reasoning. Previous work by Cywiński et al. (2025) has found that CODI's latent recurrent states (“thoughts”) do causally carry a computation's intermediate values, in a way that can be indirectly detected with LogitLens, though the thoughts themselves remained opaque. We here ask whether it is possible use activation verbalizers (AVs: NLAs and AOs) to still decode them. To this end, we train a Qwen3-8B CODI to connect to current AVs. We find that LogitLens and J-lens read values only from late layers, but AVs recover the final answer and intermediate values well above chance, including from the thoughts themselves. This suggests that the values are in fact encoded, but requires more expressivity to decode. However, we find that editing the surfaced values, rarely steers the model output towards the corresponding counterfactual answer. GitHub HuggingFace Introduction Latent reasoning models Conventional LLMs generate their chain-of-thought through a sequence of autoregressive text tokens ("verbal CoT"). In contrast, latent reasoning models use a sequence of vectors, which can amount to a reserved vocabulary, or consist in entirely opaque vectors (see Zhu et al. (2025) for a review). Currently, verbal CoT is the major source of monitorability for a model [1] . Latent reasoning however would significantly lower the monitorability since the vector's content is not obvious anymore. items.title: Even GPT-2 passes most functional global workspace tests
items.excerpt: tl;dr Anthropic’s global workspace paper (Gurnee et al., 2026) proposes five functional tests for a global workspace and, using the Jacobian lens (J-lens), finds representations in Claude that pass all five. It also finds structure supporting this set of representations in Claude that global workspace theory predicts. We test these on GPT-2 small (124M) and find it passes the tests for verbal report, internal reasoning, flexible generalization, and selectivity, but fails directed modulation. We also find almost all of the structure Gurnee et al. identified in Claude is absent. A functional global workspace would be a big deal , but we think these four tests are easily satisfied (GPT-2 small passes them), so aren't strong evidence that Claude has one (or conscious access). A case for one would have to rely on what GPT-2 lacks: directed modulation and the rest of the structure. Gurnee et al. searched for representations the model can verbalize and then found that they “rather surprisingly” pass the other tests too. However we think the four tests GPT-2 passes may mostly follow from how they and the J-lens are constructed . items.title: Why Global Trepanation?
items.excerpt: A friend asked me to investigate the following mystery: why do 5-10% of skulls from 10,000 BC to 3,000 BC, all over the world, have holes in them? Why do bone growth patterns indicate that most skull-hole-havers survived years after their holes were drilled, even though brain surgery today requires careful sterilization (and frequently, prophylactic antibiotics) to prevent fatal infections? And why did everyone stop doing this sometime around the beginning of recorded history? Was it cultural diffusion? No. Trepanation (the technical term for drilling a hole in the skull) was common across Europe and South America, with scattered cases in Africa and other continents. The Old and New Worlds had limited contact after about 10,000 BC, and most customs don’t survive for five thousand plus years with no reason. Was it good medicine? Sort of, but not in a way that entirely solves the mystery. Trepanation is an effective treatment for epidural hematoma: a patient ruptures a blood vessel in their skull, filling the cranial cavity with blood, and the pressure rises so high that it squashes various vital blood vessels and brain regions, killing the patient. Drilling a hole in the skull releases the blood, relieves the pressure, and saves the patient’s life. This is great, but these kinds of hematomas are very rare today: about 1/100,000 per year. So how do you get 5-10% of people trepanned? I think there are two reasons. First, prehistory was very violent . People were frequently…

items.title: Against Against Handover
items.excerpt: The latest bugbear is “AI successionism”, the belief that AIs should succeed humans as rulers of Earth. But some critiques fail to distinguish between two different ideas. True successionism says that AIs should take over, killing humans or steamrolling over their interests. This is very bad: a compact description of the thing that AI safety is against. Handoverism says that humans should prioritize their own interests, but that those interests may be well-served by having aligned AIs in positions of control. Some people in AI safety, including me, find this latter position plausible. We are being lumped in with the true successionists as fellow travelers in an anti-human direction ( 1 , 2 , 3 , although thanks for commenters pointing out that these essays do at least make the distinction). It may seem counterintuitive that human interests can be served by having AIs in positions of control. But I think the counterintuitiveness comes from a nationalist outlook where ‘the State is the highest expression of the life of a people’, and the role of leadership is for someone of your own ethnic group to be the leader so you can feel good about being on top. The liberal outlook is that the state exists to help individuals fulfill their goals. At the risk of desacralizing the state a little more than I mean to, it’s a service provider, dispensing coordination, public order, redistribution, and other good things. It’s fine to automate service providers. If robot garbagemen are safer…

It’s so famous, so prominent, so dominating, that the novel I think is the best war novel ever written can only point back at it from a ‘see also’ link on Wikipedia. That novel is Storm of Steel, by Ernst Jünger. You may recognize that name from 2023’s ACX book review, On the Marble Cliffs . items.title: Meetups Everywhere 2026: Times & Places
items.excerpt: By Meetups Czar Skyler: There are two laws of the ACX Meetup Czar. First, that there are a lot of ACX meetup groups. Second, that there are not enough ACX meetup groups. Twice a year, Scott advertises upcoming meetups and makes a bigger deal about it than usual. Throughout the year his meetup czar (that’s me, Skyler!) gets emails from people moving to a new city wondering if there’s an ACX group there. So the twice a year Times & Places posts are a helpful chance to check for signs of life and get an update on the local meetup communities. But the most important part is coordination. If you only go to one ACX meetup a year, we suggest you go to the fall ACX Everywhere in your city. That way if there was secretly a dozen of you all making the assumption that you were the only reader in the area, you could all show up at the fall meetup and realize the conspiracy was larger than you thought. And in fact many local ACX groups got their start by just such a rallying flag. A few were even started by a traveling reader who volunteered to run a meetup in a city they didn’t live in, but locals showed up, took the banner, and kept the meetup going. This year we have meetups planned in over a hundred and eighty cities, from Aachen, Germany to Zagreb, Croatia. Thanks to all the organizers who are putting on the individual meetups, and thank you Scott for supporting these meetups! items.excerpt: Successful companies institutionalize the knowledge of their employees; this leads to better continuity and faster on-boarding. Things like huge monorepos of useful code, internal tools, process manuals, etc. are example products of this. Young companies tend to depend on the dedication and talent of key individuals, and in maturation, must somehow make the jump to institutionalized knowledge (so that "if someone got hit by a bus" things are ok). What are some successful methods you have used or seen used to accomplish this transition? What are problems you faced (skeptics, opponents, etc.)? I am involved with an organization that is slowly growing, is about to lose key personnel, and is looking to prepare.

items.title: A Small Model Asks Better: Fine-Tuning Query Clarification for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.28686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Query clarification is essential for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems that face ambiguous user queries. We consider multi-turn grounded conversational scenarios where a user query is either ill-formed or ambiguous in the context of the prior dialog or, more interestingly, it may be well-formed but when posed against retrieved documents there are multiple relevant interpretations. The task is to recognize both such cases and then generate an appropriate clarification request to the user. We present ClariEdge, a new dataset of approximately 3,900 examples that include such ambiguous queries along with negative examples that do not require clarification. We also show that a lightweight fine-tuned LoRA achieves 96.6% classification accuracy and outperforms prompted baselines of many larger models on both classification and quality of clarification generation. Our study shows that hard negatives are an essential ingredient to separate out queries that are truly ambiguous from queries that may look ambiguous but are not (i.e., can be resolved from the context). The same LoRA achieves high performance in both pre-retrieval and post-retrieval scenarios; thus, it can be used in two places in a RAG pipeline as a check before answer generation. The ClariEdge dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibm-research/ClariEdge.

items.title: Scaling in Games: Continued Pre-Training For Embodied Agents In Diverse Virtual Worlds
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.28698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scaling data, diversity and model capacity has improved embodied learning in physical environments, where diverse experiences remain grounded in shared physical laws. Whether these gains extend to virtual worlds with different visual styles, dynamics, controls, and objectives remains unclear. We investigate this question through a controlled study of continued pre-training (CPT) across three axes: data volume, diversity, and model size. Our 120 training configurations span four model sizes from 0.8B to 27B, six data budgets from 50 to 1,600 hours, and five mixtures ranging from Minecraft-only data to diverse multi-world corpora. We assess performance and generalization using three-level validation losses and gameplay benchmarks from in-corpus worlds to unseen worlds. Our results show: (1) more data improves in-corpus performance, diversity improves transfer to related worlds with limited gains in distant worlds, and model size improves data efficiency but generalizes worse to distant worlds under single-world training; (2) we observe an early interface phase with broad cross-world benefits and a later world phase with gains narrowed to in-corpus and related worlds, and fit an empirical scaling law relating validation loss to data volume, diversity and model size; and (3) our models are competitive with Minecraft specialists and frontier models in 3D worlds, and perform best in real-time settings. However, the limits of…

items.title: SpecEvo: Speculative Evolution with Large Language Models for Cost-Efficient Scientific Discovery
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.28706v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-driven evolutionary search is a promising paradigm for scientific discovery, but existing methods remain costly and slow, often applying expensive reasoning uniformly while underusing evidence from failed, redundant, and saturated trials. We introduce Speculative Evolution (SpecEvo), a multi-LLM framework that coordinates lightweight and frontier models through continual consolidation of search evidence. Lightweight models power both parallel Speculators, which generate and refine candidate programs, and an Advisor, which distills accumulated successes, failures, and saturated directions into persistent guidance for subsequent exploration. At sparse checkpoints, a frontier-model Navigator inspects the evolving population and intervenes through synthesis, surgical refinement, or reframing according to search stagnation. This speculate-then-consolidate workflow delegates routine exploration and evidence consolidation to inexpensive models while reserving frontier reasoning for strategic interventions whose benefits extend across many subsequent low-cost evaluations. Across 176 tasks spanning four scientific and algorithmic discovery domains, SpecEvo matches or outperforms frontier-model baselines while reducing API cost by up to 80%, achieves up to 1.5x greater evaluation efficiency than cost-efficient baselines on equation discovery, and improves over the strongest CO-Bench baseline by 3.8%. These results support…

items.title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.28763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems.…

items.title: Forging More Tasks into Better Harnesses: Agentic Harness Evolution via Successive Scale Racing
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.28815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic harness evolution optimizes an agent's instructions, tools, and control flow by using its task execution experiences as evolving evidence. While more evolution tasks should intuitively improve performance, our preliminary study reveals a paradoxical failure mode: the performance of existing methods degrades as the task pool expands. Our further analysis demonstrates that this degradation stems from suboptimal evidence selection during optimization, as different evidence combinations lead to substantially different evolution outcomes. To address this issue, we propose Successive Scale Racing (SSR), a framework that adaptively searches for optimal evidence combinations in each evolution round. SSR constructs diverse evidence combinations based on the corresponding task quality and coverage, and efficiently races the resulting candidate harnesses under a small compute budget. Empirically, across three distinct benchmarks, SSR achieves state-of-the-art results in all six configurations. Notably, as the task pool grows from 40 to 200, SSR steadily improves the pass rate from 64.3% to 68.3%, while the baselines' performances all drop. Furthermore, its racing mechanism identifies near-optimal candidates while reducing validation executions by 60%.

items.excerpt: Over the past year, while Git traffic grew exponentially, 99.99999% of the Git repositories on GitHub began living in two places at once: our own data centers and Azure. The rest are among the busiest on the platform, and they’re held back by just one thing: a 25ms round trip. In an earlier blog post , we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation storage architecture: Minimize coordination Decouple storage from compute In this post, we’ll look at the immediate bridge between our old design and our new one. We’ll talk about how a change to the way our quorum serializes writes gets the busiest repositories into Azure, and how that same step opens the door to replicas that keep no persistent state of their own. How we got here The timing and shape of the move were driven by the agentic shift: rapidly growing traffic, a hard ceiling on the power capacity of our data centers and the surrounding geographical region, and physical supply chain constraints. At the beginning of our migration, the remaining capacity with all possible expansion gave us enough time to migrate safely, but not enough to do it slowly. While we had prototyped new architectural approaches for scaling Git on cloud infrastructure, changing the storage architecture and the hosting platform at the same time, under that growth, carried too much risk. Given our scale and how critical the service is to the community, we needed to sequence the work carefully: move the data first, then evolve the…

items.title: The next developer interface is ambient intelligence
items.excerpt: For most of my career, building software started with the same setup: keyboard, mouse, editor, terminal, browser, and an impressive number of tabs I was definitely going to look at later. The tools changed, but the relationship did not. Like most developers, I learned commands, memorized shortcuts, and adapted my thinking to the machine. AI is changing that relationship and not because I can prompt my way to some workable code. It’s more because the system behind it can understand a repository, choose the right model, plan work, use tools, edit files, run commands, inspect failures, and keep going within boundaries the developer controls. We’ve made it possible for a developer to describe an outcome, and GitHub Copilot can gather repository context, inspect symbols and dependencies, edit files, run tests, and revise the implementation. In the IDE, agent mode keeps that loop interactive. GitHub Copilot coding agent can take an issue into an isolated GitHub Actions-powered environment and return a pull request for review. This is not just faster coding. It is the shift from issuing commands to making intent executable. The developer still owns the outcome, but the work looks subtly different. AI-assisted development compresses that chain of events. We spend less time navigating tools and more time setting direction, supplying context, defining constraints, and reviewing evidence. items.title: Staying Evergreen: How we automated secure access and repo hygiene in a shared org
items.excerpt: Working with outside collaborators can add more work for a repository owner. You need to confirm who still needs access, change permissions as projects evolve, and archive repositories once they’ve served their purpose. To keep up, repository owners need to track collaborators, deadlines, and follow-ups for each repository. As a project grows, that manual housekeeping becomes harder to keep up with and easier to defer. We faced this problem in a shared organization where GitHub employees (“Hubbers”) collaborate with customers and partners on product trials and professional services engagements. Our answer was Evergreen , a GitHub App built with native GitHub features. The workflows below exhibit a pattern you can adapt for your own organization. Meet Evergreen Evergreen is a GitHub App that automates organization hygiene through two workflows: Outside collaborator access reviews. Every quarter, each repo’s outside collaborators are reviewed. Keep who you need, and everyone else is removed. Stale repository detection and archival. Repos with no human activity past a threshold get flagged, warned, and (if still untouched) archived. Two design principles shaped everything: Fail secure. If nobody responds to an access review, we don’t leave access in place and hope for the best. We revoke it. items.title: Drug company gifts, meals, and payments to doctors lead to worse prescribing, review of 93 studies finds
items.excerpt: Key findings Pharmaceutical marketing aimed at doctors, from gifts to meals and payments, may increase inappropriate prescribing and the quantity and cost of prescriptions. Conflict‐of‐interest policies that restrict or manage interactions between pharmaceutical companies and doctors can limit prescribing of inappropriate drugs and overprescribing. Gifts, payments, free meals, and other marketing ploys by pharmaceutical companies heavily influence doctors to prescribe more drugs, choose less appropriate treatments, and drive up prescription costs, according to a systematic review of 93 studies. These prescribing choices can expose patients to drugs that offer fewer benefits, cause more side effects or are unnecessary, while increasing health system costs. The review , published today [October 9] in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, found that policies restricting interactions between drug companies and doctors were associated with better prescribing choices, lower costs, and possibly fewer prescriptions. “Overall, when doctors have more contact with drug company promotion, prescribing tends to become less appropriate, more frequent, and more expensive,” said co-author Dr. Lisa Bero, an affiliate professor at the University of Colorado Anschutz Center of Bioethics and Humanities. “This is problematic for a number of reasons, and it matters because it directly affects patient care.” Dr. Quinn Grundy, director of the World Health Organization Collaborating Centre for…

items.title: Hormone-disrupting chemical mixtures linked to excess childhood weight
items.excerpt: Key findings Multiple hormone-disrupting chemicals were linked to obesity from childhood through adolescence. Prenatal exposure to metals, organochlorine pesticides, and PFAS was linked to higher obesity. Childhood exposure to phenols and certain phthalates was linked to more body fat in adolescence. Children exposed during pregnancy and early life to combinations of chemicals that disrupt hormones and metabolism may face a greater risk of excess weight that persists into adolescence, a new study suggests. Published this month [September 2026] in Environment International , the study followed 1,301 mother-child pairs from six European birth cohorts. Researchers measured prenatal and childhood exposure to 45 endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) across nine chemical classes. These included per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances ( PFAS), phthalates , pesticides , polychlorinated biphenyls ( PCBs), flame retardants, metals, parabens, and phenols, including bisphenol A (BPA) and triclosan. Researchers found that greater exposure to certain combinations of EDCs was associated with higher BMI. They also found links to more body fat and higher odds of overweight. About 28% of the children had overweight or obesity at age 8, rising to about 30% by age 15. The findings add to growing evidence linking chemical exposures during critical stages of development to obesity risk. items.title: FAA Training Records Detail Toxicology and Autopsy Procedures Following Fatal Aviation Accidents
items.excerpt: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) released 20 pages of training materials concerning the collection, processing, and analysis of biological evidence following fatal aviation accidents. The records were released on October 12, 2023, in response to Freedom of Information Act request, which sought presentation slides and a syllabus for the training course Mass Fatalities for Medicolegal Professionals (TDA403). In its response, the FAA stated: “Presentation slides were discovered during the search for records pertaining to this request. No syllabus was found, all training in this course was derived from these slides as presented.” The released materials include presentations concerning the FAA’s Bioaeronautical Sciences Research Laboratory (BSRL) and its Autopsy Program Team, both associated with the Civil Aerospace Medical Institute (CAMI) in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. These programs support investigations of fatal aviation accidents by coordinating autopsy documentation and conducting forensic toxicological examinations. According to the FAA, its aviation safety responsibilities include collecting medical and pathological information to help identify factors contributing to aircraft accidents. A 2020 FAA technical report, Comparative Evaluation of Forensic Toxicology Findings, 2012–2016, further documents how CAMI’s forensic laboratories and Autopsy Program Team support both the FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB).
